Bacteria achieve genetic variation through horizontal gene transfer (HGT) via three mechanisms:

1. Transformation: Uptake of naked dsDNA fragments from the environment by a competent cell, integrated via homologous recombination. Discovered by Frederick Griffith (1928) in Streptococcus pneumoniae.

2. Conjugation: Direct, contact-dependent DNA transfer from a donor (F+) to recipient (F-) via a sex pilus, driven by the Fertility (F) plasmid. The F+ cell extends a pilus; relaxosome enzymes nick the F plasmid at oriT; the single strand transfers via rolling circle replication, converting the recipient to F+. Hfr strains arise when the F plasmid integrates into the chromosome, enabling chromosomal gene transfer.

3. Transduction: Bacteriophage-mediated transfer. Generalized: During the lytic cycle, bacterial DNA is accidentally packaged into phage heads. Specialized: During lysogenic-to-lytic transition, adjacent bacterial genes (e.g., gal, bio) are excised alongside phage DNA.

✓

1. Insect and Pest Resistance: Bt Crops incorporating cry genes from Bacillus thuringiensis; delta-endotoxin proteins solubilize in the insect's alkaline midgut, forming lethal pores, conferring resistance in cotton and brinjal.

2. Herbicide Tolerance: 'Roundup Ready' crops incorporate a bacterial EPSPS synthase gene resistant to glyphosate for effective weed control.

3. Nutritional Fortification: Golden Rice, engineered with three biosynthetic genes (two from daffodil, one from Erwinia) to synthesize β-carotene; transgenic potatoes with the AmA1 gene for higher essential amino acids.

4. Abiotic Stress Tolerance: Genes for osmoprotectants (proline, glycine betaine) or heat shock proteins helping crops tolerate drought, salinity, and temperature extremes.

5. Delayed Fruit Ripening: Flavr Savr tomatoes engineered with antisense RNA silencing the polygalacturonase gene, delaying softening and extending shelf life.

✓

Structural Components: Structural genes lacZ (β-galactosidase), lacY (permease), lacA (transacetylase); regulatory sequence Promoter (P), Operator (O), and regulatory gene lacI encoding the Lac Repressor.

Regulation Mechanism: Negative Control (no lactose): The lacI gene produces an active repressor that binds the operator, blocking RNA polymerase — the operon stays OFF. Induction (lactose present): Lactose converts to allolactose (the inducer), which binds the repressor causing dissociation from the operator, turning the operon ON.

Catabolite Repression (Positive Control by Glucose): High Glucose: Adenylate Cyclase is inhibited, lowering cAMP; without the cAMP-CAP complex bound near the promoter, lac transcription stays minimal. Low Glucose/High Lactose: Adenylate Cyclase activates, raising cAMP; the cAMP-CAP complex bends DNA and helps RNA polymerase bind, triggering robust transcription — ensuring glucose is used preferentially when available.

✓

Definition: Chromosome mapping determines the relative locations of genes on a chromosome and the linear distances between them, derived from recombination frequencies or conjugation transfer times.

1. Interrupted Mating Conjugation (Hfr × F⁻ Mapping): Discovered by Jacob and Wollman. An Hfr donor with wild-type alleles is mixed with an F⁻ recipient carrying recessive markers; the Hfr chromosome transfers sequentially at constant speed from oriT. Samples are removed at intervals and blended to interrupt transfer, then plated on selective media. Plotting gene arrival time yields a map measured in minutes (the E. coli chromosome corresponds to a 100-minute circular map).

2. Generalized Transduction Mapping: Genes close together are more likely co-packaged into a single phage head (co-transduction); measuring co-transduction frequency reveals fine-structure genetic distances.

3. Transformation Mapping: The frequency of joint transformation (co-transformation) of two donor markers provides fine-scale map distances for closely linked genes.

Definition: A cloning vector is a small, stably maintained DNA molecule used to carry foreign genetic material into a host cell for independent replication and expression.

Essential Requirements: An origin of replication; a selectable marker gene; unique restriction sites (MCS).

Types of Cloning Vectors:

  • Plasmids: Small circular dsDNA (capacity up to 10 kb; e.g., pBR322, pUC19).
  • Bacteriophage Vectors: Derived from Lambda phage (capacity 10–20 kb).
  • Cosmids: Hybrid vectors combining plasmid sequences with lambda cos sites (capacity 30–45 kb).
  • Bacterial Artificial Chromosomes (BACs): Based on the F-factor plasmid (capacity 100–300 kb).
  • Yeast Artificial Chromosomes (YACs): Linear vectors with yeast centromeric, telomeric, and ARS sequences (capacity 100–1000 kb).

Detailed Description of pBR322: Constructed by Bolivar and Rodriguez (1977); 4,361 bp; origin from plasmid pMB1 (15–20 copies/cell); two selectable markers — amp^R and tet^R genes; unique restriction sites — inserting DNA at the BamHI/SalI site within tet^R inactivates tetracycline resistance (insertional inactivation), so recombinants remain amp^R but become tet^S, identifiable by replica plating.

✓

Definition: The MHC is a dense, highly polymorphic cluster of cell-surface antigen-presenting proteins. In humans it is the Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA) complex on chromosome 6; in mice, the H-2 complex.

MHC Class I: A heavy alpha chain non-covalently associated with beta-2-microglobulin; expressed on virtually all nucleated cells and platelets; presents endogenous antigens (viral/tumor proteins) to Cytotoxic T Lymphocytes (CD8+).

MHC Class II: A heterodimer of alpha and beta transmembrane glycoprotein chains; restricted to professional Antigen-Presenting Cells (dendritic cells, macrophages, B lymphocytes); presents exogenous (engulfed) antigens to Helper T Lymphocytes (CD4+).

MHC Class III: Encodes non-membrane proteins in immune cascades — complement factors (C2, C4, Factor B) and inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, lymphotoxin).

Clinical Importance: MHC genes are the most polymorphic known in vertebrates, ensuring broad microbial peptide presentation; MHC compatibility is a major determinant in tissue/organ transplantation, where mismatches trigger graft rejection.

✓

Definition: Monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) are monospecific, uniform antibodies produced by a single B-lymphocyte clone, identical in structure and binding affinity.

Production via Hybridoma Technology (Köhler and Milstein, 1975):

  1. Immunization: A mouse is injected with a target antigen to stimulate an immune response.
  2. Isolation of B-Cells: Antibody-producing plasma B lymphocytes are harvested from the spleen.
  3. Cell Fusion: B cells (finite lifespan) are fused with immortalized myeloma cells (lacking HGPRT) using PEG.
  4. Selection: Culturing in HAT medium kills unfused spleen and myeloma cells; only fused hybridoma cells survive, combining immortality with antibody production.
  5. Screening and Cloning: Hybridomas are screened via ELISA; positive clones are isolated and expanded.

Applications: Diagnostic tools (pregnancy tests, ELISA, western blotting, blood typing) and therapeutic agents (Trastuzumab for breast cancer, Rituximab for lymphoma, Infliximab for rheumatoid arthritis).

✓

Definition: Interferons (IFNs) are cytokines synthesized by host cells in response to viral infection, parasites, and tumors, establishing an 'antiviral state' in neighboring cells.

Classification: Type I — IFN-alpha (leukocytes) and IFN-beta (fibroblasts), binding the IFNAR receptor for antiviral/antiproliferative effects. Type II — IFN-gamma (activated T cells, NK cells), an immunomodulator activating macrophages and enhancing MHC expression. Type III — IFN-lambda, acting via distinct receptors mainly on epithelial tissues.

Mechanism of Antiviral Action: An infected cell detects viral nucleic acids and secretes IFNs; these bind receptors on neighboring cells, activating the JAK-STAT pathway; this induces Interferon-Stimulated Genes (ISGs), producing key antiviral enzymes — 2',5'-Oligoadenylate Synthetase (activates RNase L to degrade RNA) and Protein Kinase R (halts protein translation).

Clinical Applications: Treating chronic Hepatitis B/C, multiple sclerosis (IFN-beta), and malignancies like hairy-cell leukemia.

✓

Definition: An allergy (hypersensitivity Type I reaction) is an exaggerated immune response to normally harmless allergens (pollen, dust mites, dander, foods).

1. Sensitization Phase (Initial Exposure): An allergen is processed by APCs and presented to CD4+ Th2 helper cells; Th2 cells secrete IL-4/IL-13, signaling B lymphocytes to switch antibody production to IgE; allergen-specific IgE binds high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells/basophils, sensitizing them.

2. Effector Phase (Re-exposure): The allergen cross-links surface-bound IgE on sensitized mast cells, triggering degranulation — releasing histamine, leukotrienes, prostaglandins, and heparin.

Pathological Effects: Smooth muscle contraction, increased vascular permeability, vasodilation, and mucus hypersecretion — ranging from mild symptoms (rhinitis, hives) to severe systemic anaphylaxis (airway constriction, rapid blood pressure drop).

✓

Definition: Immunoglobulins (Igs/antibodies) are antigen-binding glycoproteins synthesized by plasma B lymphocytes, with a Y-shaped structure of four polypeptide chains held by disulfide bonds.

Chain Composition (150 kDa monomer): Two identical Heavy (H) chains (~50 kDa each) and two identical Light (L) chains (~25 kDa each, kappa or lambda type).

Structural Domains: Variable Regions (V_H, V_L): N-terminal ends, containing hypervariable Complementarity-Determining Regions (CDRs) forming the antigen-binding paratope. Constant Regions (C_H, C_L): C-terminal ends; the heavy chain constant region determines the immunoglobulin class (IgG, IgM, IgA, IgD, IgE) and mediates effector functions.

Proteolytic Cleavage Products: Papain Digestion yields two identical Fab (antigen-binding) fragments and one Fc (crystallizable) fragment. Pepsin Digestion yields a single divalent F(ab')₂ fragment.

✓

Lymphocytes (Adaptive Immunity):

  • T-Lymphocytes: Mature in the thymus, mediate cell-mediated immunity. Helper T-cells (CD4+) recognize MHC II antigens and secrete cytokines activating B-cells, cytotoxic T-cells, macrophages. Cytotoxic T-cells (CD8+) recognize MHC I antigens and destroy infected/tumor cells via perforins and granzymes. Regulatory T-cells suppress autoreactive responses.
  • B-Lymphocytes: Mature in bone marrow; upon antigen encounter, differentiate into antibody-secreting Plasma Cells and long-lived Memory B-cells.
  • Natural Killer (NK) Cells: Innate lymphoid cells targeting tumor/virus-infected cells without prior sensitization, via antibody-dependent cellular cytotoxicity.

Phagocytic Cells (Innate Immunity):

  • Neutrophils: Most abundant WBCs (60–70%), first responders using reactive oxygen species and lysosomal enzymes.
  • Macrophages and Monocytes: Engulf debris and act as professional Antigen-Presenting Cells.
  • Dendritic Cells: Bridge innate and adaptive immunity by displaying antigens to naive T-cells.

Granulocytes: Eosinophils protect against parasites and mediate allergic reactions; Basophils and Mast Cells express high-affinity IgE receptors, triggering degranulation during allergy and anaphylaxis.

✓

Definition: DNA fingerprinting (DNA profiling/typing) establishes genetic identity by analyzing unique DNA variations. Developed by Sir Alec Jeffreys (1984), relying on hypervariable VNTRs and STRs.

Principle and Methodology: While 99.9% of human DNA is identical across individuals, the remaining 0.1% shows polymorphic satellite DNA. Steps: (1) DNA extraction from biological samples; (2) Cleavage with restriction endonucleases; (3) Separation by gel electrophoresis; (4) Transfer via Southern Blotting; (5) Hybridization with labeled VNTR probes; (6) Detection of unique band patterns.

Applications:

  1. Forensic Investigations: Matching suspect DNA to crime-scene evidence.
  2. Paternity and Maternity Disputes: Comparing inherited VNTR allele patterns.
  3. Pedigree Analysis and Wildlife Conservation: Assessing genetic diversity, preventing inbreeding, curbing illegal poaching.
  4. Taxonomy and Phylogenetics: Establishing evolutionary relationships.
  5. Medical Diagnostics: Monitoring bone marrow transplant engraftment and detecting genetic disorders.
✓

1. Innate Immunity (Non-Specific Defense): Present from birth, providing immediate protection.

  • Physical Barriers: Skin, mucous membranes lining respiratory/GI/urogenital tracts.
  • Chemical Barriers: Low gastric pH, lysozyme in tears/saliva, defensins, fever.
  • Cellular Barriers: Phagocytes (neutrophils, macrophages, monocytes) using Pattern Recognition Receptors; Natural Killer cells targeting infected cells.
  • Cytokine/Complement Systems: Interferons protecting neighboring cells; the complement cascade forming membrane attack complexes.

2. Acquired (Adaptive) Immunity: Develops after antigen exposure, with specificity, diversity, and memory.

  • Humoral Immunity (B-Cell Mediated): B-cells differentiate into antibody-secreting plasma cells; immunoglobulins neutralize toxins, opsonize bacteria, activate complement.
  • Cell-Mediated Immunity (T-Cell Mediated): Helper T-cells (CD4+) recruit other immune cells; Cytotoxic T-cells (CD8+) induce apoptosis in infected/malignant cells.
  • Immunological Memory: Memory B and T cells enable a faster, stronger secondary response upon re-exposure.
▢

CHE 303

Chemistry — Previous Year Questions

Organised into three parts, matching the paper pattern — Part 1 Inorganic, Part 2 Organic, Part 3 Physical.

✓

MO Diagram for O₂ (16 electrons): For O₂, F₂ and Ne₂, the σ(2pz) orbital lies below the π(2px,2py) orbitals (negligible s–p mixing). Filling order: σ(2s)² σ*(2s)² σ(2pz)² π(2px)²π(2py)² π*(2px)¹π*(2py)¹ σ*(2pz)⁰.

Magnetic Behaviour: By Hund's rule, the two degenerate π* orbitals are each singly occupied, giving two unpaired electrons — O₂ is therefore paramagnetic, famously confirmed by liquid O₂ being attracted into a magnetic field (a fact simple Lewis structures cannot explain).

Bond Order: Bonding electrons = 8 (2+2+2+2), antibonding = 4 (2+1+1). Bond order = (8−4)/2 = 2 (a double bond, consistent with O=O).

N₂: Here s–p mixing is significant, so π(2p) lies below σ(2pz). Filling: σ(2s)²σ*(2s)²π(2px)²π(2py)²σ(2pz)². All electrons paired → diamagnetic; bond order = (8−2)/2 = 3 (triple bond), explaining N₂'s very high bond dissociation energy.

O₂⁺ (dioxygenyl): One electron removed from π*, leaving one unpaired electron → paramagnetic; bond order = (8−3)/2 = 2.5 (shorter, stronger bond than O₂).

O₂⁻ (superoxide): One electron added to π*, giving three π* electrons (one unpaired) → paramagnetic; bond order = (8−5)/2 = 1.5 (longer, weaker bond than O₂).

✓

Splitting in an Octahedral Field: Six ligands approach along the ±x, ±y, ±z axes. Orbitals pointing directly at the ligands (dz², dx²−y² — the eg set) experience greater electrostatic repulsion and are raised in energy, while orbitals pointing between the ligands (dxy, dxz, dyz — the t2g set) are lowered.

Δₒ (10Dq): The energy gap between eg and t2g is called the octahedral crystal-field splitting energy, Δₒ. Relative to the barycentre (average energy), t2g lies at −0.4Δₒ and eg at +0.6Δₒ, so that the total is conserved: 3(−0.4Δₒ) + 2(0.6Δₒ) = 0.

CFSE (Crystal Field Stabilization Energy): The net energy lowering of the d-electron configuration relative to the (hypothetical) unsplit, spherically symmetric field, calculated by summing electron occupancies × their orbital energies (and adding pairing-energy penalties where relevant).

Example — d⁶ ion: High spin (weak field, e.g. [CoF₆]³⁻): t2g⁴eg² → CFSE = 4(−0.4Δₒ) + 2(0.6Δₒ) = −0.4Δₒ. Low spin (strong field, e.g. [Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺): t2g⁶eg⁰ → CFSE = 6(−0.4Δₒ) = −2.4Δₒ (plus an extra pairing-energy cost for the additional electron pairs formed compared to the high-spin case).

✓

Colour: When a ligand field splits the d-orbitals, an electron can be promoted from t2g to eg (a d–d transition) by absorbing a photon of energy equal to Δₒ. The wavelength absorbed depends on Δₒ, which in turn depends on the metal ion, its oxidation state, and the ligand's position in the spectrochemical series. The observed colour is complementary to the wavelength absorbed — e.g. [Ti(H₂O)₆]³⁺ absorbs in the yellow-green region and appears violet.

Magnetic Properties: Whether a complex is high spin or low spin — and hence how many unpaired electrons it has — depends on the relative magnitudes of Δₒ and the pairing energy P. Weak-field ligands (e.g. F⁻, H₂O; Δₒ < P) favour high spin (more unpaired electrons, strongly paramagnetic), while strong-field ligands (e.g. CN⁻, CO; Δₒ > P) favour low spin (fewer unpaired electrons, weakly paramagnetic or diamagnetic).

Examples: [Fe(H₂O)₆]²⁺ (weak field, high spin, t2g⁴eg², 4 unpaired e⁻, strongly paramagnetic, pale green) vs. [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻ (strong field, low spin, t2g⁶eg⁰, 0 unpaired e⁻, diamagnetic, yellow) — the same metal ion showing dramatically different colour and magnetism purely due to the ligand field.

✓

Electronic Configuration: Lanthanides (Ce–Lu) have the general configuration [Xe]4fn5d0–16s². The 4f orbitals are progressively filled and are effectively shielded by the filled 5s²5p⁶ subshells, so 4f electrons take little part in bonding.

Oxidation States: The dominant, most stable oxidation state is +3 (Ln³⁺), formed by loss of 6s² and one 5d/4f electron. A few ions also show +2 or +4 where this gives an extra-stable f⁰, f⁷ or f¹⁴ configuration — e.g. Ce⁴⁺ (f⁰), Eu²⁺ (f⁷), Tb⁴⁺ (f⁷), Yb²⁺ (f¹⁴).

Magnetic Properties: Because 4f electrons are shielded from the ligand environment, orbital angular momentum is not quenched (unlike in d-block ions), so the spin-only formula fails. Magnetic moments are instead given by μeff = g√[J(J+1)] BM, where g is the Landé g-factor and J is the total angular momentum quantum number — this formula agrees well with experimental values for most lanthanides (Sm³⁺ and Eu³⁺ being notable exceptions due to low-lying excited states).

Basis of Separation: Because of the lanthanide contraction, ionic radii decrease only very slightly and smoothly across the series, making chemical separation extremely difficult by classical methods. Modern separation relies on ion-exchange chromatography (using a complexing eluent like citrate or EDTA, which forms complexes of subtly different stability with each Ln³⁺, causing them to elute in sequence) and solvent extraction, both of which exploit these small but systematic differences in ionic size/complex stability.

✓

Structure: Both proteins contain a heme prosthetic group — an Fe²⁺ ion held in the centre of a porphyrin ring, coordinated to four pyrrole nitrogens equatorially and to a histidine residue (the 'proximal histidine') of the protein axially; the sixth coordination site binds O₂. Myoglobin is a single polypeptide chain (monomeric), found in muscle tissue for O₂ storage. Haemoglobin is a tetramer of four such subunits (2α + 2β chains), found in red blood cells for O₂ transport.

Oxygen-Binding Properties: Myoglobin shows a simple, hyperbolic O₂-binding curve (non-cooperative, single binding site). Haemoglobin shows a sigmoidal (S-shaped) curve because binding of O₂ at one subunit induces a conformational change (T-state → R-state) that increases the O₂ affinity of the remaining subunits — this is called positive cooperativity (allosteric behaviour).

Oxygen Transport: In the lungs (high pO₂), haemoglobin binds O₂ efficiently due to cooperativity, becoming nearly saturated. In peripheral tissues (lower pO₂, higher CO₂/H⁺, the Bohr effect), haemoglobin's O₂ affinity decreases, favouring O₂ release exactly where it is needed. This switching behaviour, impossible for the simple monomeric myoglobin, makes haemoglobin an efficient long-range O₂ transporter while myoglobin acts as a local O₂ reservoir.

✓

Statement: In an ionic crystal, the coordination number adopted by the cation is determined by the ratio of the cation radius to the anion radius, r⁺/r⁻ — the cation surrounds itself with as many anions as can touch it without the anions touching each other, which sets a minimum permissible radius ratio for each coordination geometry.

Radius-Ratio Ranges and Predicted Geometry:

  • 0.155 – 0.225 → Coordination number 3, trigonal planar
  • 0.225 – 0.414 → Coordination number 4, tetrahedral
  • 0.414 – 0.732 → Coordination number 6, octahedral
  • 0.732 – 1.000 → Coordination number 8, cubic (body-centred)

Application: For example, in NaCl, r(Na⁺)/r(Cl⁻) ≈ 0.53, which falls in the octahedral range, correctly predicting NaCl's rock-salt (6:6 octahedral) structure. In CsCl, the larger Cs⁺ gives r⁺/r⁻ ≈ 0.93, correctly predicting the 8:8 cubic structure. The rule is a useful first approximation, though it fails for compounds with significant covalent character.

✓

Structure: Borazine, B₃N₃H₆, is a six-membered ring of alternating boron and nitrogen atoms, each bearing one hydrogen, isostructural with benzene (C₆H₆) — hence its nickname 'inorganic benzene'. The ring is planar with B–N bond lengths intermediate between single and double bonds, indicating some π delocalization.

Bonding: Each nitrogen contributes its lone pair into a delocalized π system across the ring (similar to benzene's π cloud), while each boron is electron-deficient. However, unlike benzene's uniform electron distribution, borazine's π system is polarized — electron density is concentrated more on the electronegative nitrogen atoms and less on boron, making the ring's bonding less symmetric than benzene's.

Comparison with Benzene: Despite the structural similarity, borazine is chemically much more reactive than benzene. Because of the B–N bond polarity, borazine readily undergoes addition reactions (e.g. with HCl, giving B-Cl/N-H addition products) rather than the electrophilic substitution reactions characteristic of true aromatic benzene — showing that borazine's 'aromaticity' is significantly weaker than benzene's.

✓

Preparation: Silicones are prepared by hydrolysis of alkyl/aryl chlorosilanes, RnSiCl4−n (obtained from the Rochow process, reacting Si with RCl over a Cu catalyst). Hydrolysis gives silanols (RnSi(OH)4−n), which then undergo condensation polymerization, eliminating water to form long chains linked by Si–O–Si bonds.

Structure: The resulting polymer has a repeating –[R₂SiO]n– backbone (the siloxane linkage), with organic R groups (usually methyl or phenyl) projecting from each silicon. Using RSiCl₃ or SiCl₄ in the mix introduces cross-linking, giving resins or rubbers instead of simple linear chain oils.

Properties: High thermal and oxidative stability (strong Si–O bond), water repellency (hydrophobic organic groups), chemical inertness, good electrical insulation, and flexibility over a wide temperature range.

Applications: Lubricants and hydraulic fluids, sealants and adhesives, waterproofing coatings, electrical insulation, and biocompatible medical implants/prosthetics.

✓

Variable Oxidation States: The (n−1)d and ns orbitals of transition metals are very close in energy, so electrons can be successively removed from both without a large energy penalty, allowing a range of accessible oxidation states (e.g. Mn shows +2 to +7).

Colour: Partially filled d-orbitals allow d–d electronic transitions upon absorption of visible light (in the presence of a ligand field that splits the d-orbitals); the transmitted/reflected complementary colour is observed. Ions with d⁰ or d¹⁰ configurations (no possible d-d transition) are typically colourless.

Magnetic Behaviour: Unpaired d electrons give rise to paramagnetism; the number of unpaired electrons (hence magnetic moment) depends on the dⁿ configuration and the ligand field strength (high spin vs low spin).

Complex Formation: Transition metal ions are small and highly charged, giving high charge density, and possess vacant (n−1)d, ns, np orbitals available to accept lone pairs from ligands (Lewis bases) — this combination makes them excellent Lewis acids, readily forming coordination complexes.

✓

Molybdenum: Ore: Molybdenite (MoS₂). Extraction: The ore is concentrated by froth flotation, roasted in air to MoO₃, which is then reduced with hydrogen at high temperature to give the metal. Important Compounds: MoO₃ (used as a catalyst and pigment), MoS₂ (a solid lubricant).

Tungsten: Ores: Wolframite ((Fe,Mn)WO₄) and Scheelite (CaWO₄). Extraction: Ore is converted to sodium tungstate (Na₂WO₄) by fusion with Na₂CO₃, then treated with acid to precipitate tungstic acid (H₂WO₄), which is calcined to WO₃ and reduced with hydrogen to the metal. Important Compounds: WO₃ (used in tungsten filaments after reduction, and as a catalyst), WC (tungsten carbide, extremely hard, used in cutting tools).

Vanadium: Ores: Vanadinite and Patronite. Extraction: Roasting the ore with NaCl/Na₂CO₃ gives sodium vanadate, which is acidified to precipitate 'red cake' (ammonium/sodium polyvanadate), calcined to V₂O₅, and reduced with Ca or Al (Goldschmidt process) to give the metal. Important Compounds: V₂O₅ (an important industrial catalyst in the Contact Process for H₂SO₄ manufacture).

✓

General Approach to Structure Elucidation from PMR:

  1. Degree of Unsaturation: Calculate from the molecular formula (DoU = C − H/2 + N/2 + 1) to check for rings/π bonds/aromatic rings.
  2. Number of Signals: Each chemically non-equivalent set of protons gives one distinct signal — protons related by molecular symmetry appear as a single signal.
  3. Chemical Shift (δ, ppm): Indicates the electronic environment of a proton — e.g. alkyl C–H (δ 0.9–1.5), allylic/benzylic C–H (δ 2–3), O–CH (δ 3.3–4.5), vinyl =CH (δ 5–6.5), aromatic Ar–H (δ 6.5–8), aldehyde CHO (δ 9–10), carboxylic acid COOH (δ 10–13, broad). Downfield shifts arise from proximity to electronegative atoms or ring-current deshielding.
  4. Multiplicity (n+1 rule): A proton's signal is split into (n+1) lines by n equivalent neighbouring protons on adjacent carbons (spin-spin coupling), with relative intensities following Pascal's triangle.
  5. Integration: The relative area under each signal gives the relative number of protons contributing to it.

Worked Example — Ethyl acetate (C₄H₈O₂, δ): Three signals are observed: a singlet at δ 2.0 (3H, CH₃CO–, no neighbouring H), a quartet at δ 4.1 (2H, –OCH₂–, split by the adjacent CH₃'s 3 protons), and a triplet at δ 1.25 (3H, –CH₃, split by the adjacent CH₂'s 2 protons) — the pattern of 3 signals with a 3:2:3 integration ratio, together with the quartet-triplet coupling, confirms the ethyl-ester connectivity.

✓

1. Benzene → Aniline: (i) Conc. HNO₃/H₂SO₄ (nitration) → Nitrobenzene; (ii) Sn/HCl or H₂/Pd (reduction) → Aniline.

2. Ethanol → Acetic Acid: Oxidation with acidified KMnO₄ or K₂Cr₂O₇/H⁺, heat.

3. Benzene → Benzaldehyde: (i) CH₃Cl/anhydrous AlCl₃ (Friedel-Crafts) → Toluene; (ii) CrO₂Cl₂ (Étard reaction) or side-chain chlorination followed by hydrolysis → Benzaldehyde.

4. Propan-1-ol → Propanoic acid → Propanamide: (i) Oxidation (KMnO₄/H⁺) → Propanoic acid; (ii) SOCl₂ → Propanoyl chloride; (iii) NH₃ (excess) → Propanamide.

5. Acetone → Isopropyl alcohol → Propene: (i) NaBH₄ or H₂/Ni (reduction) → Isopropyl alcohol; (ii) Conc. H₂SO₄, heat (dehydration) → Propene.

6. Phenol → Salicylaldehyde: Reimer-Tiemann reaction — CHCl₃/NaOH, then acidify.

✓

Open-Chain Structure: D-glucose, C₆H₁₂O₆, is an aldohexose — a straight chain with an aldehyde group at C1 and hydroxyl groups at C2–C6, with the D-configuration fixed at C5.

Evidence for the Open-Chain Structure:

  • Reacts with HCN to give a cyanohydrin (confirms a carbonyl group).
  • Reduces Tollens' and Fehling's reagents (confirms an aldehyde, not a ketone).
  • Forms an oxime with NH₂OH and a pentaacetate with acetic anhydride (confirms 5 –OH groups plus the carbonyl).
  • Forms an osazone with excess phenylhydrazine.

Cyclic (Pyranose) Structure: Glucose actually exists predominantly as a six-membered hemiacetal ring formed between the C1 aldehyde and the C5 –OH group, generating a new stereocentre at C1 (the anomeric carbon), giving α- and β-anomers. This explains why glucose shows only weak, incomplete aldehyde reactions (e.g. does not give the Schiff's test directly) and forms only a monomethyl acetal with one equivalent of methanol/HCl (not a normal acetal).

Mutarotation: When pure α-D-glucose (specific rotation +112°) or pure β-D-glucose (+18.7°) is dissolved in water, its optical rotation gradually changes and settles at an equilibrium value of about +52.7°. This occurs because the ring opens reversibly to the open-chain aldehyde form and recloses randomly to give an equilibrium mixture of ~36% α and ~64% β anomers — this spontaneous change in optical rotation is called mutarotation.

✓

Aromaticity: All three are five-membered heterocycles satisfying Hückel's rule (6π electrons: 4 from two C=C double bonds + 2 from the heteroatom's lone pair delocalized into the ring). However, the degree of aromaticity differs based on how readily the heteroatom's lone pair is donated into the ring: Thiophene > Pyrrole > Furan. This order follows the electronegativity of the heteroatom — oxygen (most electronegative) holds its lone pair most tightly and donates it least effectively into the ring (weakest aromaticity, most reactive/least stable to electrophiles), while sulfur (least electronegative, larger, more polarizable) donates its lone pair most effectively into the ring system (strongest aromatic character among the three).

Orientation of Electrophilic Substitution: In all three, electrophilic substitution occurs preferentially at the 2-position (α-position, adjacent to the heteroatom) rather than the 3-position (β). This is because attack at C2 generates a resonance-stabilized cationic intermediate with three contributing resonance structures (including one where the positive charge is stabilized by direct donation from the heteroatom lone pair), whereas attack at C3 gives an intermediate with only two resonance structures and no direct heteroatom stabilization — making the α-substituted transition state considerably more stable.

✓

Epimers: Two diastereomeric sugars that differ in configuration at exactly one stereocentre (other than the anomeric carbon). For example, D-glucose and D-galactose are epimers, differing only at C4; D-glucose and D-mannose are epimers differing only at C2.

Anomers: Cyclic sugars that differ in configuration specifically at the anomeric carbon (C1 in aldoses, C2 in ketoses) — the new stereocentre created upon ring closure. α- and β-D-glucose are anomers.

Mutarotation: The spontaneous change in optical rotation observed when a pure anomer is dissolved in water, as it equilibrates (via the open-chain form) to a mixture of both anomers (see previous answer for detail).

Interconversion of Glucose and Fructose: In dilute alkali, glucose, fructose and mannose interconvert via a common enediol intermediate (the Lobry de Bruyn–Alberda van Ekenstein rearrangement) — this is why glucose, fructose, and mannose all give the same osazone with excess phenylhydrazine (they share identical configurations at C3, C4, C5).

Other Key Reactions: Both sugars reduce Fehling's/Tollens' reagents (fructose does so via this same base-catalyzed isomerization to an aldose); both are reduced by NaBH₄ to sugar alcohols (glucose → sorbitol; fructose → a mixture of sorbitol and mannitol, since a new stereocentre is created at C2 on reduction).

✓

Synthesis of Amino Acids:

  • Strecker Synthesis: An aldehyde reacts with NH₃/HCN to form an aminonitrile, which is then hydrolyzed to give the α-amino acid.
  • Gabriel–Phthalimide/Malonic Ester Route: Phthalimidomalonic ester is alkylated with an alkyl halide, then hydrolyzed and decarboxylated to give a substituted amino acid.

Properties of Amino Acids: Amphoteric (contain both acidic –COOH and basic –NH₂ groups); exist predominantly as zwitterions (⁺H₃N–CHR–COO⁻) in aqueous solution; each has a characteristic isoelectric point (pI) — the pH at which the molecule carries no net charge; undergo condensation to form peptide (amide) bonds, releasing water.

Determining the N-Terminal Amino Acid:

  • Sanger's Method: The peptide is treated with 1-fluoro-2,4-dinitrobenzene (DNFB/Sanger's reagent), which reacts with the free α-amino group of the N-terminal residue. Complete acid hydrolysis then releases a yellow DNP-amino acid, identified by chromatography, revealing which amino acid was N-terminal.
  • Edman Degradation: The peptide is treated with phenyl isothiocyanate (PITC), which reacts with the N-terminal amino group to form a phenylthiocarbamyl derivative; mild acid then selectively cleaves only the N-terminal residue (as a PTH-amino acid) without hydrolyzing the rest of the peptide, allowing repeated cycles to sequence successive residues from the N-terminus.
✓

1. Free-Radical Polymerisation: Initiated by a radical initiator (e.g. benzoyl peroxide), which homolytically generates a radical that adds to a monomer's double bond, propagating a chain of radical addition steps until termination (combination/disproportionation). Example: Polyethylene from ethylene monomer.

2. Ionic Polymerisation: Proceeds via a carbocation (cationic, initiated by a Lewis acid such as BF₃/H₂O, favoured by electron-donating substituted alkenes) or carbanion (anionic, initiated by a strong base/organometallic, favoured by electron-withdrawing substituted alkenes) intermediate. Example: Polyisobutylene from isobutylene via cationic polymerisation.

3. Condensation Polymerisation: Bifunctional monomers react stepwise, each step releasing a small molecule (commonly water), building the polymer chain through repeated condensation reactions. Example: Nylon-66, from hexamethylenediamine and adipic acid, with loss of water at each amide linkage.

4. Ziegler-Natta Polymerisation: Uses a coordination catalyst (typically TiCl₄ combined with an aluminium alkyl co-catalyst, Al(C₂H₅)₃) that coordinates the monomer and inserts it in a controlled, stereoregular fashion. Example: Isotactic polypropylene, with all methyl groups on the same side of the chain, giving a highly crystalline, strong polymer — impossible to achieve with free-radical polymerisation of propylene.

✓

Quinoline — Preparation (Skraup Synthesis): Aniline is heated with glycerol, concentrated H₂SO₄, and an oxidizing agent (e.g. nitrobenzene). Glycerol dehydrates to acrolein under the acidic conditions; aniline undergoes Michael addition to acrolein, followed by cyclization and oxidative aromatization, to give quinoline.

Quinoline — Reactions: Being a fused benzene-pyridine system, the benzenoid ring undergoes electrophilic substitution preferentially at C5/C8, while the pyridine-like ring (electron-poor due to the ring nitrogen) undergoes nucleophilic substitution at C2/C4.

Indole — Preparation (Fischer Indole Synthesis): Phenylhydrazine is condensed with an aldehyde or ketone to form a phenylhydrazone, which undergoes a [3,3]-sigmatropic rearrangement under acid catalysis (e.g. ZnCl₂ or H₂SO₄), followed by cyclization and loss of NH₃, to give the indole ring.

Aromatic Character: Quinoline is a fully aromatic 10π-electron bicyclic system, behaving much like naphthalene/pyridine combined. Indole is also aromatic (10π electrons across the fused benzene and pyrrole rings), with the pyrrole-type nitrogen's lone pair delocalized into the ring system (analogous to pyrrole), making indole's C3 position highly reactive towards electrophiles (much like pyrrole's α-position reactivity, transposed by the fusion).

✓

Malonic Ester Synthesis: Diethyl malonate, CH₂(COOEt)₂, has an acidic α-CH₂ (flanked by two ester groups) that is readily deprotonated by NaOEt to form a stabilized enolate. This enolate is alkylated with an alkyl halide (R–X) to give a mono- or di-substituted malonic ester. Subsequent hydrolysis and heating causes decarboxylation of one carboxyl group, ultimately yielding a substituted acetic acid, RCH₂COOH (or R₂CHCOOH for double alkylation).

Acetoacetic Ester Synthesis: Ethyl acetoacetate, CH₃COCH₂COOEt, similarly has an acidic α-CH₂ between a ketone and an ester group. Its enolate (formed with NaOEt) is alkylated with R–X, and subsequent hydrolysis/decarboxylation removes the ester's carboxyl group, giving a substituted methyl ketone, CH₃COCH₂R.

Synthetic Utility: Both syntheses are powerful methods for building longer-chain carboxylic acids or ketones with precise substitution patterns from a simple two-carbon (or three-carbon) building block, by choosing the appropriate alkyl halide(s) for the alkylation step(s) — including using dihalides to build cyclic products.

✓

The Reaction: The Diels-Alder reaction is a [4+2] cycloaddition between a conjugated diene (in the reactive s-cis conformation) and a dienophile (typically an electron-poor alkene/alkyne, activated by an electron-withdrawing group), forming a new six-membered ring with two new σ-bonds and one new π-bond.

Mechanism: The reaction is concerted — both new σ-bonds form simultaneously in a single, cyclic transition state, with no discrete intermediate. It is classified as a thermally allowed pericyclic (cycloaddition) reaction under the Woodward-Hoffmann rules, proceeding in a suprafacial-suprafacial fashion on both components.

Stereochemical Features: Because it is concerted and suprafacial-suprafacial, the reaction is highly stereospecific — the relative configuration (cis/trans) of substituents on the dienophile is fully retained in the product. The reaction also shows endo selectivity (the 'endo rule') — the kinetically favoured product places electron-withdrawing substituents on the dienophile oriented toward the diene π-system (endo), due to favourable secondary orbital interactions in the transition state.

Example: 1,3-Butadiene (diene) + maleic anhydride (dienophile) → cis-cyclohex-4-ene-1,2-dicarboxylic anhydride, with the anhydride ring retaining its original cis relationship and adopting the endo orientation.

✓

Definition: The chemical potential of component i, μᵢ, is defined as the partial molar Gibbs free energy: μᵢ = (∂G/∂nᵢ)T,P,nj≠i — the change in total Gibbs free energy of a system per mole of component i added, at constant temperature, pressure, and amounts of all other components.

Relationship with Thermodynamic Variables: Starting from the total differential of G for a multicomponent, open system: dG = −SdT + VdP + Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ. At constant T and P, this reduces to dG = Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ, showing μᵢ as the driving force for mass transfer of component i. Similarly, μᵢ can be expressed as a partial derivative of U, H, or A with respect to nᵢ under the appropriate constant natural variables (e.g. μᵢ = (∂U/∂nᵢ)S,V,nj).

Significance: Chemical potential plays the same role for mass transfer that temperature plays for heat transfer: matter spontaneously flows from a region of higher μᵢ to lower μᵢ, until μᵢ is equal everywhere (equilibrium). This is the fundamental basis of the phase equilibrium condition (μᵢ equal in every phase in which i is present) and of chemical equilibrium (Σ νᵢμᵢ = 0 for reactants/products at equilibrium).

✓

Definition: Fugacity, f, is an 'effective' or 'corrected' pressure that accounts for the non-ideal behaviour of real gases, defined such that the chemical potential of a real gas retains the same simple mathematical form as for an ideal gas: μ = μ° + RT ln(f/f°). As pressure P → 0, f → P (all gases behave ideally at low pressure).

Derivation: From dμ = RT d(ln f) at constant T, and the general thermodynamic relation dμ = VmdP at constant T, we get d(ln f) = (Vm/RT)dP. Integrating between an ideal reference state and the real state gives: RT ln(f/P) = ∫₀ᴾ (Vm − Vm,ideal) dP, where the integrand is the deviation of the real molar volume from ideal-gas molar volume (RT/P). Defining the fugacity coefficient γ = f/P, this integral gives ln γ directly from experimental P-V-T (or equation-of-state) data.

Calculation: Using a truncated virial equation, PVm = RT(1 + BP/RT) (B = second virial coefficient), the integral gives ln γ = BP/RT, so f = P·exp(BP/RT). For example, given B and P/T for a specific gas, f is obtained directly by substitution — for a gas at low-to-moderate pressure with a negative B (attractive interactions dominate), f < P (γ < 1).

✓

The Steady-State Approximation (SSA): For a reactive intermediate I formed and consumed in a multi-step mechanism, since I is highly reactive and present only in a very low, roughly constant concentration during the bulk of the reaction, we assume its net rate of formation is approximately zero: d[I]/dt ≈ 0.

General Procedure:

  1. Write the rate expressions for formation and consumption of the intermediate from each elementary step in which it appears.
  2. Set the net rate of change of [I] to zero and solve algebraically for [I] in terms of the concentrations of stable species.
  3. Substitute this expression for [I] back into the rate expression for the overall product-forming step, eliminating the unmeasurable intermediate concentration.
  4. Simplify to obtain the final observed rate law, expressed only in terms of reactant/product concentrations and rate constants.

Overall Order: The overall order of reaction is determined by inspecting the exponents on concentration terms in the final derived rate law — this is not necessarily equal to the molecularity of any single step, and may even be a non-integer or fractional order (as commonly arises when a square-root term appears from a pre-equilibrium or chain mechanism, e.g. the H₂+Br₂ reaction below).

✓

Mechanism (Chain Reaction):

  • Initiation: Br₂ + hν → 2Br•
  • Propagation (1): Br• + H₂ → HBr + H•
  • Propagation (2): H• + Br₂ → HBr + Br•
  • Inhibition: H• + HBr → H₂ + Br•
  • Termination: 2Br• → Br₂

Applying the Steady-State Approximation to the reactive intermediates [H•] and [Br•] (setting d[H•]/dt = 0 and d[Br•]/dt = 0), solving the resulting simultaneous equations for [H•] and [Br•] in terms of [H₂], [Br₂] and [HBr], and substituting into the rate of HBr formation, d[HBr]/dt = k₁[Br•][H₂] + k₂[H•][Br₂] − k₋₁[H•][HBr], gives the classic experimentally-observed rate law:

d[HBr]/dt = k[H₂][Br₂]1/2 / (1 + k′[HBr]/[Br₂])

The characteristic square-root dependence on [Br₂] arises directly from the initiation/termination steps (2Br• → Br₂ being a second-order process in [Br•]), and the inhibiting effect of the product HBr (denominator term) arises from the reverse inhibition step — both features that a simple integer-order rate law could never explain, which is why this reaction is a classic textbook example for the steady-state method.

✓

Concentration Cell: A galvanic cell in which both electrodes are chemically identical, but differ only in the concentration of the electrolyte solution in contact with them; the EMF arises purely from the free energy of dilution (mixing), not from any chemical reaction difference.

Without Transference (electrodes reversible to the ion, connected via a salt bridge, no liquid junction): For a cell such as M | Mn+(a₁) ‖ Mn+(a₂) | M, the EMF is derived directly from the Nernst equation for each half-cell: E = (RT/nF) ln(a₂/a₁) (with a₂ > a₁, current flows to equalize concentrations).

With Transference (direct contact between the two solutions, a liquid junction present): Here an additional liquid-junction potential (Ej) arises at the boundary due to unequal mobilities of the cation and anion diffusing across the junction. The overall measured EMF becomes: Ewith transference = 2t₋(RT/nF) ln(a₂/a₁) (for a cell where t₋ is the transport number of the anion), which is smaller in magnitude than the 'without transference' value.

Liquid-Junction Potential: Comparing the two derived expressions, Ej = (t₊ − t₋)(RT/nF) ln(a₂/a₁), calculated directly once the transport numbers t₊ and t₋ of the electrolyte's ions are known — Ej vanishes only when t₊ = t₋ (equal ionic mobilities).

✓

The Problem: Unimolecular gas-phase reactions (A → products) are experimentally first order at high pressure but shift to second order at low pressure — a puzzle, since a 'unimolecular' process should intuitively always be first order.

Lindemann's Mechanism: Molecules are first activated to an energized state A* by bimolecular collision, which can either be de-activated by a further collision or can go on to react unimolecularly:

  • Activation: A + A → A* + A (rate constant k₁)
  • De-activation: A* + A → A + A (rate constant k₋₁)
  • Reaction: A* → Products (rate constant k₂)

Derivation (Steady-State on A*): Setting d[A*]/dt = k₁[A]² − k₋₁[A*][A] − k₂[A*] = 0, and solving for [A*] = k₁[A]² / (k₋₁[A] + k₂), the rate of product formation is:

Rate = k₂[A*] = k₁k₂[A]² / (k₋₁[A] + k₂)

Limiting Cases: At high pressure (high [A]), k₋₁[A] ≫ k₂, so Rate ≈ (k₁k₂/k₋₁)[A] — first order, matching experiment. At low pressure (low [A]), k₂ ≫ k₋₁[A], so Rate ≈ k₁[A]² — second order, also matching experiment. This successfully explains the pressure-dependent order that a simple one-step mechanism could not.

✓

Derivation: For a multicomponent system, the total Gibbs free energy can be written as G = Σᵢ nᵢμᵢ (Euler's theorem for a first-order homogeneous function). Taking the total differential: dG = Σᵢ nᵢ dμᵢ + Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ. But we also know from the fundamental equation that dG = −SdT + VdP + Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ. Comparing these two expressions for dG (both must be equal), the Σᵢ μᵢ dnᵢ terms cancel, leaving:

−SdT + VdP = Σᵢ nᵢ dμᵢ

At constant temperature and pressure, this simplifies to the Gibbs-Duhem equation: Σᵢ nᵢ dμᵢ = 0.

Physical Significance: The equation shows that the chemical potentials of the components of a mixture cannot vary independently of one another at constant T and P — a change in the chemical potential (and hence activity/composition) of one component necessarily constrains how the chemical potential of the other component(s) must change. It is widely used as a thermodynamic consistency check for experimentally measured activity coefficients (e.g. in vapour-liquid equilibrium data) — a self-consistent data set must satisfy the Gibbs-Duhem relation.

✓

The Theory: Transition State Theory (Eyring theory) proposes that as reactants approach each other, they pass through a high-energy, unstable configuration called the activated complex (transition state, X‡), which is assumed to be in a rapid, quasi-equilibrium with the reactants before proceeding irreversibly to products: A + B ⇌ X‡ → Products.

Derivation: Treating the equilibrium A + B ⇌ X‡ with an equilibrium constant K‡ = [X‡]/([A][B]), and assuming the activated complex decomposes to products with a universal frequency factor (kBT/h) (derived from statistical mechanics, where kB is Boltzmann's constant and h is Planck's constant), the rate of reaction is:

Rate = (kBT/h) K‡ [A][B], giving the rate constant k = (kBT/h) K‡ = (kBT/h) exp(−ΔG‡/RT)

where ΔG‡ is the Gibbs free energy of activation. Expanding ΔG‡ = ΔH‡ − TΔS‡ gives k = (kBT/h) exp(ΔS‡/R) exp(−ΔH‡/RT).

Role of Activation Energy: The activation enthalpy ΔH‡ (closely related to the Arrhenius activation energy, Ea ≈ ΔH‡ + RT) represents the energy barrier that must be surmounted to reach the transition state — a higher ΔH‡ means fewer molecules have sufficient energy at a given temperature, giving a smaller rate constant, exactly as captured by the exponential term.

✓

Setup: Consider a particle of mass m confined to a 1-D box of length L, where the potential V = 0 inside the box (0 < x < L) and V = ∞ outside (so ψ must vanish at the walls). The time-independent Schrödinger equation inside the box is:

−(ħ²/2m) d²ψ/dx² = Eψ

Solution: This is a standard second-order differential equation with general solution ψ(x) = A sin(kx) + B cos(kx), where k = √(2mE)/ħ. Applying the boundary conditions ψ(0) = 0 (forces B = 0) and ψ(L) = 0 (requires sin(kL) = 0, so kL = nπ for n = 1, 2, 3, ...), we obtain the quantized wavefunctions:

ψₙ(x) = √(2/L) sin(nπx/L),   Eₙ = n²h²/8mL²,   n = 1, 2, 3, ...

(the normalization constant √(2/L) is found by requiring ∫₀ᴸ |ψ|² dx = 1.)

Significance of the Wave Function: ψ itself has no direct physical meaning, but |ψ|² (the Born interpretation) gives the probability density of finding the particle at a given position x. The quantization of energy (Eₙ ∝ n²) arises directly and solely from the boundary conditions imposed by confinement — a purely quantum-mechanical result with no classical analogue, and the model correctly predicts phenomena like zero-point energy (E₁ ≠ 0) and nodes in higher wavefunctions.

✓

The Equation: Arrhenius empirically observed that the rate constant of most reactions varies with temperature according to:

k = A e−Ea/RT

where A is the pre-exponential (frequency) factor, Ea is the activation energy, R is the gas constant, and T is the absolute temperature. This form can be justified from collision theory (A relates to collision frequency and steric factor) or from Transition State Theory (as shown in the TST derivation above).

Effect of Temperature on k: Taking the natural log, ln k = ln A − Ea/RT — the rate constant increases exponentially, non-linearly, with increasing temperature, because a larger fraction of molecular collisions possess energy exceeding Ea as T rises (from the Boltzmann distribution of molecular energies). Even a modest temperature rise can dramatically increase k when Ea is large.

Determining Ea (Graphical Method): Differentiating ln k with respect to (1/T) gives d(ln k)/d(1/T) = −Ea/R — meaning a plot of ln k versus 1/T gives a straight line with slope = −Ea/R (from which Ea is calculated) and intercept = ln A. Alternatively, using the two-temperature form ln(k₂/k₁) = −(Ea/R)(1/T₂ − 1/T₁), Ea can be calculated directly from rate constants measured at just two different temperatures.
